title: 830/1427: the recall
dramatic_question: The summons reaches you on the road out of Herat. What do you do?

situation.where: Herat, and the road out of it

invariants.text: In 830/1427 the Ḥurūfī Aḥmad-i Lur tried to kill Shāhrukh as he left the congregational mosque in Herat and was killed on the spot.
After the attempt Shāhrukh arrested prominent figures with suspected Ḥurūfī ties, among them Qāsim-i Anvār, Maʿrūf-i Khaṭṭāt and Ibn Turka.

The pages Melvin-Koushki gives do not say what tied Ibn Turka to the Ḥurūfiyya; the only Ḥurūfī contact they name is the family's dream-interpretation visits to Fażl Allāh, which he says imply no Ḥurūfī leaning.

prose: Shāhrukh's men are taking those the court suspects of Ḥurūfī ties: Qāsim-i Anvār, the calligrapher Maʿrūf-i Khaṭṭāt, and you.

You have just left Herat. Your lettrist works never name the Ḥurūfīs, and the charge of Sufi bias made against you in 1422 is read by Melvin-Koushki as probably meant to tie you to them. He reads the purge as Shāhrukh consolidating the state, and notes that the attempt may have been staged by the ruler himself, a conjecture the game does not treat as fact.
A summons comes after you. You can obey it, you can turn away, or you can look to the people who have helped you before.

choices.label: Obey the recall and go back to Herat, whatever waits there.
costs: You lose your post and property, and are imprisoned, then exiled.
Torture is reported; Melvin-Koushki names the second apology as the main source for the exile period.
choices.feedback: The record has you recalled, imprisoned, stripped of position and property, tortured and exiled. Melvin-Koushki's page gives no source for that sentence and names the second apology as the main source for the exile period, so the account is your word to another judge. What you do once in custody, including your surviving letter 27 to Amīr Fīrūzshāh, is the next scene.

choices.label: Turn away from Herat and try to reach a governor who will shelter you.
costs: You keep more of what you have: your livelihood falls by less than the record has it fall. Running reads as guilt, and exposure rises steeply.
choices.feedback: No source has him refusing a recall. The record has him summoned back and exiled; running would only change how it looks. The game returns you to the record. What you gained and paid here stays in your ledger; the story then rejoins the record.

choices.label: Obey the recall, but first ask Bāysunghur, who favoured you, to speak for you.
costs: Needs Bāysunghur's favour already earned, and spends it.
You lose less than the record has you lose. Asking a prince to speak for a suspect adds to your exposure.
choices.feedback: The sources have Bāysunghur addressed for help only years later, in the second apology, which asks his intercession to little real effect. No source has him speaking for you in 1427. The game returns you to the record: the exile comes anyway. What you gained and paid here stays in your ledger; the story then rejoins the record.
